At the big pond in Evergreen Cemetery. There have been a number of frogs moving as I walk, but this was the first one this season that I was able to id, as a Green Frog. This one was along the shore near the only small wooden bridge at this pond. I differentiated this from a Bull Frog but the dorsolateral ridges to frog seemed to be showing.

The entire time that I watched the frog it only moved once. The rest of the time it was stationary. Not that is too surprising. Only the head, eyes, and tympanum were above water.

The one time the frog moved was when I moved forward a step which caused it to move forward a step. It didn't flee, instead it made a quick movement and went back to sitting.

It looked to be about 3"-4" long with a head that appears to be 1" wide. As might be clear in the picture, the frog was dark green, probably because it was wet.

The weather when I observed the frog was 50f, 7mph, and overcast. It felt raw.

description: The green frog is a secondary consumer, eating anything from spiders, to crayfish, to insects, to other frogs. Green frogs are most obviously recognized by the bright green sides of their heads. They typically have a dark green or brown back, although this coloring can be varied. In order to distinguish the green frog from the bullfrog, one can look at the ridged lines on the frogs back, called glandular folds. On bullfrogs these lines circles around the ear, on green frogs they go straight down the back. Green frogs begin as eggs, before hatching quickly in about a week. They are then tadpoles, with a tail and no legs, before becoming a froglet, which has legs and a tail. Finally, the frog sheds the tail, and becomes a mature adult. The frog observed is a mature adult. I was not able to sex it. Green frogs are found around inland water sources, such as a stream, creak, lake, or pond. They can also be found in deep mud when hibernating, and in damp woods near water. A predator of the green frog is the Northern Water Snake, a competitor is the American Bullfrog.

This organism can be identified as a green frog by its green head/neck and brown lower body/legs, with darker patches just visible beneath the mud on its back and legs. It has smooth skin without any warts. It can be distinguished from the American bullfrog by the presence of 2 raised ridges running down either side of its back, known as dorsolateral folds. Green frogs eat algae, bugs, and occasionally other frogs or snakes, making them secondary consumers. The life cycle of the green frog begins as an egg which is laid in an aquatic environment. Eggs hatch after no longer than a week, giving way to the tadpole stage, in which the frogs live entirely within water. After 3-22 months as a tadpole, the frogs undergo metamorphosis into the adult stage, after which they can live on land and reproduce. It takes 4-5 years for the frogs to grow to their maximum adult size. The frog pictured appears to be an adult, as it was found on land with fully developed legs. It is about 4 inches long, so it is most 4 years old or older, as adult green frogs typically range from 3-5 inches long. This individual is most likely a male, as it has large tympanums that appear to be bigger than its eyes. Green frogs can be found in habitats such as marshes, swamps, ponds, lakes, and streams. Other organisms that can usually be found in these habitats may include various insects, herbaceous plants, algae, trees, snakes, and beavers. This one was located along the bank of a small stream within a forest. Green frogs may be preyed upon by turtles such as the snapping turtle (Chelydra serpentina) during their tadpole stage. Their prey includes insects such as the spangled skimmer dragonfly (Libellula cyanea) and a potential competitor is the American bullfrog (Lithobates catesbeianus).
